name: bug

attributes.attribute: a syllable found in the names of meddlesome sprites
a creature that blocked the roofing of St Trinian's church
a saint whose church on the Isle of Man was haunted
linked by some scholars to the bog and the Otherworld

sources: Killip, Margaret. The Folklore of the Isle of Man. London: B. T. Batsford, Ltd., 1975, 106.

Ross, Anne. “Lindow Man and the Celtic Tradition.” In The Lindow Man: The Body in the Bog, edited by I. M. Stead, J. B. Bourke, and Don Brothwell, 162–169. Ithaca, N.Y.: Cornell University Press, 1986.

text: The word bug names a Celtic folkloric figure. Variations of this syllable appear in many sprite names. These include bug-a-boo, bugbear and bullbeggar. The forms bogle, bogie, bogan, boggart and boogyman also appear. The word boge occurs in other Indo-European languages with the sense of god. Some scholars use this to argue that such spirits are diminished deities. Other scholars reject the link outright. Yet others connect bug to the bog, a liminal opening to the Otherworld. On the Isle of Man a bug or buggane haunted a church. The church dates from about the twelfth century and is tied to St Ninian. It was called St Trinian's here. The church never got a roof. Each time roofers climbed up, a coarse-haired apparition destroyed their work. A tailor sewed the roof onto the rafters to defeat the creature's magic. The buggane chased him away and threw its own head at him. The buggane vanished after that and the roofing project stopped.

okr.objective: Explain the bug as a Celtic folkloric figure whose name syllable marks meddlesome sprites.
key_results: The syllable bug appears in many sprite names such as bug-a-boo and boggart.
The word boge means god in other Indo-European languages.
Some scholars argue these spirits are diminished deities, while others reject the claim.
A buggane haunted St Trinian's church and stopped the roofing each time.
